what_its_for: Diazoxide is used to treat low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) that keeps coming back, especially when it is caused by the body making too much insulin. It works by telling your pancreas to release less insulin, which helps keep your blood sugar at a safe level.
how_to_take: Take diazoxide by mouth exactly as your doctor tells you. It comes as a liquid (suspension) or a capsule. Shake the liquid well before each use and measure it carefully with the measuring device that comes with your medicine — do not use a regular kitchen spoon. You can take it with food or milk to help reduce stomach upset. Take it at the same times every day to keep your blood sugar steady.
dosing: The dose is different for each person and is based on your weight, age, and how your body responds to the medicine. Your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly adjust it. A common adult dose is 3 to 8 milligrams per kilogram of body weight per day, split into 2 or 3 doses. For infants and newborns, the dose is usually 8 to 15 milligrams per kilogram per day, split into 2 or 3 doses. Never change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. But if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are not sure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store diazoxide at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep it away from light and heat. Keep the bottle tightly closed. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not store it in the bathroom. Do not use it after the expiration date printed on the label. Ask your pharmacist how to safely throw away medicine you no longer need.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking diazoxide because it can cause your blood sugar to drop dangerously low. Avoid standing up too quickly, as diazoxide can cause dizziness or lightheadedness. Do not take diuretics (water pills) such as hydrochlorothiazide without talking to your doctor, as they can interact with diazoxide and affect your blood sugar and blood pressure. Avoid activities that require full alertness, like driving or operating heavy machinery, until you know how this medicine affects you.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: fast or irregular heartbeat, sudden weight gain or swelling in your hands, feet, or face, shortness of breath, signs of very high blood sugar (extreme thirst, frequent urination, blurred vision, confusion), unusual hair growth especially in children, severe nausea or vomiting, stomach pain, or skin rash. Also call your doctor if your blood sugar readings are consistently too high or too low.
when_it_works: Diazoxide usually starts working within 1 hour of taking a dose. You and your doctor will check blood sugar levels regularly to see how well it is working. It may take a few days to a few weeks before your doctor finds the right dose that keeps your blood sugar in a safe range. Do not stop taking it on your own even if you feel better.
special_populations: Children and Infants: Diazoxide is used in newborns, infants, and children but must be dosed carefully by weight. Children may experience unusual hair growth on the face and body (hypertrichosis), which usually goes away after stopping the medicine. Pregnant or Breastfeeding Women: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Diazoxide can affect the baby and may cause problems during labor and delivery. It may pass into breast milk, so talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Older Adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects like low blood pressure and fluid retention. Kidney or Liver Problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you have kidney or liver disease. Always tell your doctor and pharmacist about all medical conditions and all medicines you are taking.
